clinicalPearls: Caused by several Borrelia species (such as Borrelia hermsii in North America and Borrelia duttonii in Africa) and transmitted by the bite of soft (argasid) Ornithodoros ticks, whose bites are brief and painless and often not recalled
Exposure is classically linked to sleeping in rustic cabins or dwellings harbouring rodent-associated ticks, so a careful environmental history is important
After an incubation of about a week there is abrupt high fever, rigors, headache, myalgia and arthralgia lasting a few days, followed by an afebrile interval and then one or more relapses
The relapsing pattern reflects successive waves of spirochaetaemia as the organism undergoes antigenic variation to evade the developing antibody response
Diagnosis is often made by seeing spirochaetes on a peripheral blood film (thick and thin films, ideally taken during a febrile spike) using Giemsa or Wright staining
Tetracyclines such as doxycycline are the mainstay of treatment, with beta-lactams as alternatives, and treatment is usually given empirically once the diagnosis is suspected
A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is common on starting treatment, so patients should be observed and supported through it
reference.pathophysiology: Relapsing fever borreliae are spirochaetes inoculated during the brief feeding of soft ticks. They multiply in the bloodstream to produce high-grade spirochaetaemia, which drives the febrile episodes. As host antibodies clear the dominant serotype, the organism switches its surface antigens through programmed antigenic variation, allowing an antigenically distinct population to expand and cause a further febrile relapse; this cycle repeats, producing the characteristic relapsing pattern. High spirochaetal loads can involve the spleen, liver, central nervous system and heart, and the sudden release of bacterial products on antibiotic-induced lysis provokes the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
additionalInvestigations: Thick and thin peripheral blood films taken during fever to demonstrate spirochaetes
PCR of blood for Borrelia species where available
Serology, interpreted with caution owing to cross-reactivity and variable performance
Full blood count, which may show thrombocytopenia
Lumbar puncture if central nervous system involvement is suspected
redFlags: Neurological features such as meningism, cranial nerve palsies or altered consciousness
Myocarditis with heart failure or arrhythmia
Marked haemorrhagic tendency or profound thrombocytopenia
Severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hypotension after the first antibiotic dose
Pregnancy, in which disease and vertical transmission carry added risk
reference.prognosis: With appropriate antibiotics tick-borne relapsing fever generally has a good prognosis and low mortality, though the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be severe; untreated or complicated disease, particularly with cardiac or neurological involvement, carries higher risk.
pitfalls: Not examining blood films during a febrile spike, when spirochaetaemia is highest
Failing to warn about and manage the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
Missing the diagnosis because the painless soft-tick bite is not recalled
Attributing recurrent fevers to a relapsing viral illness or malaria without a film
Overlooking central nervous system or cardiac complications in severe cases
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with a tetracycline such as doxycycline as the mainstay, with a beta-lactam (penicillin or ceftriaxone) as an alternative, often started empirically once the diagnosis is suspected
Use parenteral ceftriaxone or penicillin where there is central nervous system involvement
Anticipate and support the patient through a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first antibiotic dose, with observation and supportive measures
Provide supportive care with antipyretics and fluid replacement
Monitor the full blood count for thrombocytopenia and assess for cardiac, hepatic and neurological involvement
Advise environmental measures such as rodent and tick control and avoiding tick-infested rustic dwellings to prevent reinfection
